en: Recorded by the Disciple Guanding of the Teachings of the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai during the Sui Dynasty.
Part Two: Contemplating the Pervasiveness of the Destruction of Dharmas through the Entry into Emptiness via the Provisional. This consists of three sections. First, the Explanation.
First, the contemplation of the provisional;
second, clarifying the essence of contemplation;
third, clarifying its stages.
Regarding the "provisional" [afflictions],
these refer to greed, hatred, delusion, and pride;
they are called the dull fetters and are also termed the three primary poisons.
Traversing the three realms constitutes ten [stages].
Furthermore, regarding the three realms, there are nine grounds;
within each ground, there are nine grades.
These comprise eighty-one categories in total.
All are capable of moistening karma and causing rebirth within the three realms;
even those who have attained the first fruit must still undergo seven more returns before their afflictions are exhausted.
It is like a lamp that burns most brightly just before it goes out.
Although he may have desire, he does not engage in sexual misconduct with women;
although he may have anger, he does not harm living beings by tilling the earth.
Although there may be those who are ignorant and do not contemplate the reality of the nature [of phenomena],
the power of the precepts concurrent with the Path functions spontaneously in this way;
therefore, it is called "right affliction."
Unlike the delusions of view, which are vast and unbounded, giving rise to attachment upon contact with objects,
those termed "contemplative" (saṃtīraka) derive their name from their understanding;
yet, when first contemplating the Truth, it is shallow and still obstructed by residual phenomena.
Later, when one reflects deeply, these delusions are immediately eliminated;
therefore, they are called "delusions of reflection.
The Saṃkhyas say:
The craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is called "greed" (*rāga*), while that for the higher realms is called "attachment" (*tṛṣṇā*).
The author of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* (Treatise on Establishment) challenges this terminology,
arguing that there is greed for the dhyānas with outflows in the higher realms, and there is desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*) for the lower realms.
Both craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and greed (*lobha*) apply universally;
for what reason is there this partial judgment?
If it is said that greed is heavy in the lower realms and light in the higher realms, [then...]
Could that which is light greed not be non-greed?
This is also a single category;
it is simply that the Buddha sometimes speaks of them separately according to specific conditions.
Since provisional designations have no fixed nature, how can they be treated as a single uniform case?
One need only summon the afflictions and then destroy them;
why trouble oneself with disputing over craving and attachment?
For example, when clearing away filth, the primary concern is merely to remove the impurity; detailed discernment is not urgent.
Entering the Way requires skillful means (*upāya*) as its essential;
names and marks are merely incidental.
If you wish to know the Abhidharma and the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* in full detail,
you may seek them there;
what I am discussing here is the contemplation of emptiness and the provisional.
Second, regarding the clarification of the contemplation of the essence:
if, within the gate of arising and ceasing, one first employs analytical wisdom (*vikalpa-jñāna*) to sever the afflictions of views,
and subsequently again employs analytical wisdom through repeated reflection to sever the afflictions of latent tendencies (*bhāvanā-heya*).
In the gate of non-arising and non-ceasing, one first employs the essence to perceive and enter emptiness;
subsequently, one again employs the essence to contemplate and deliberate repeatedly,
without resorting to any other path.
Now, regarding those who realize emptiness through the provisional nature of desire:
as each of the nine grades of the afflictions of desire arises,
there are three types of provisional existence for each.
Just as a woman has six desires:
namely, desire for color, desire for physical form and appearance,
desire for deportment and gestures, and desire for speech and voice.
The desire for the smooth and soft is the desire for personal characteristics;
such are the various distinctions.
These six desires, if encountered by one who practices, can defile the sense faculties.
The internal movement of blood and vessels manifests externally as the appearance of craving;
this has not yet been severed even by those who have attained the first fruit of the path,
let alone by ordinary worldlings.
Nanda’s residual habits were such that,
seeing a woman in the midst of the assembly whom he had previously conversed with,
his lingering desire was stirred.
How much more so for one who is a true messenger!
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"One should not preach the Dharma while perceiving the marks of a woman's body that can give rise to thoughts of desire."
If one grasps these signs,
and the sense faculty of the mind moves toward sensory objects to give rise to a desirous mind,
this is a provisional construction based on causes.
When thoughts arise in a continuous succession without interruption, they eventually lead to action;
this is "conceptual continuity" (*prabandha-prajñapti*).
This is because a mind characterized by desire is distinct from a mind devoid of desire.
This is precisely the provisional nature of mutual dependence.
Being false and unreal, one ultimately does not reckon it as a fundamental principle.
Thus one contemplates this mind of desire.
Does it arise from the sense organ, or does it arise from the object?
Does it arise from both together, or independently?
If it arises from the sense organ...
If it were not in relation to an object, the mind should arise by itself.
If it arises from an object, since the object is something else, what concern does it have with me?
If it were produced by both together, two minds should arise simultaneously.
If it were produced without a cause, that would be untenable.
Examining desire through the four alternatives,
one finds that desire has no place of origin.
Having neither place of origin nor place of departure,
it is without desire, without categories, without coming, and without going;
it is ultimately empty and quiescent.
When a person of sharp faculties contemplates in this manner,
they contemplate one grade of the provisional and remove one portion of the real, so that clarity becomes manifest.
Even if they have not yet applied the four *siddhāntas* in practice, [the result is achieved].
By faithfully turning toward the Dharma and skillfully harmonizing calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā),
one immediately attains correspondence.
One eliminates a single grade of afflictions and manifests a portion of the Truth, and so forth.
If a person of dull faculties contemplates within the establishment of causes,
and the first stage has not yet passed, they further contemplate within the continuum:
does the preceding thought perish and give rise [to the subsequent one]?
Does it arise from non-extinction?
Does it arise from both extinction and non-extinction?
Or does it arise from neither extinction nor non-extinction?
If it arises from that which has ceased,
that which has ceased cannot produce it; if it arises from that which has not ceased, [it likewise cannot produce it].
If there is no cessation, there is no arising.
If there were arising from either cessation or non-cessation,
it would contradict their inherent natures.
If one were to depart from arising,
this would be impossible;
within the four propositions, there is neither desire nor the four [propositions] themselves.
When contemplating in this manner, one should immediately attain entry into the twofold emptiness of both phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*).
If one does not enter, one should skillfully practice according to the four *siddhāntas*.
If one still does not enter despite such cultivation, one should further apply contemplation within the context of mutual dependence; the analogy may be understood as before.
As it is with the first chapter,
so it is with the subsequent eight chapters;
as it is with the ninefold refutation of sensual desire, so it is with all others.
The same applies to the nine grades of the destruction of hatred, delusion, and pride;
this can be understood by analogy and need not be recorded in detail.
The manifestation of the nine grades of reality is precisely the non-arising of principle.
The exhaustion of the nine grades of afflictions is the non-arising of the cause;
the non-origination of the fruit in the desire realm is the non-arising of the fruit.
Because they do not arise, they do not cease.
This refers to the "patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and so forth.
Question:
Are the afflictions of the desire realm necessarily of nine grades?
Answer:
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, the path of non-obstruction suppresses [the defilements] and the path of liberation abandons them;
this treatise discusses only the nine grades.
According to the Abhidharma, [defilements] are suppressed by two paths— the path of skillful means (upāyamārga) and the path of superior progress (viśeṣamārga)—
severed by the path of non-obstruction (ānantaryamārga),
and realized by the path of liberation (vimuktimārga).
This is the state of realization free from delusion,
which is frequently employed in various sutras;
for now, we shall rely upon it.
If one enters contemplation from the perspective of conventional designations,
the untainted mind is swift and does not emerge from contemplation to sever [afflictions], regardless of their grade;
whereas in the path of cultivation, there is leisurely progression and the possibility of employing skillful means.
Skillfully practicing the turning toward the Dharma of faith,
one enters the stage of superior progress;
if one repeatedly makes such superior progress, [one attains further advancement].
One should know that the ranks and categories are also numerous;
how could they be limited to only nine?
These nine are merely stated as a broad classification.
Next, regarding the destruction of the nine grades of the form realm:
one may employ either mundane knowledge or untainted knowledge.
Just as those liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) likewise lack worldly dhyāna,
yet achieve the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) solely through the untainted (anāsrava),
so too those in the first fruit who lack dhyāna [achieve their goal through the untainted].
Cultivation through repeated reflection refers to the application of untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna).
As for those who are liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta),
they may employ either untainted wisdom or mundane wisdom (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
For now, we shall rely on worldly knowledge and take those who have attained dhyāna as our primary focus.
When first practicing dhyāna, one breaks through the obstacles of conditioned phenomena and gives rise to the concentration of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*).
By breaking through the obstacle of nature (*dharmāvaraṇa*), one immediately gives rise to the meditative concentration of form (*rūpasamādhi*).
Therefore, it is said that the obstacle of phenomena (*vastvāvaraṇa*) pertains to the future, while the obstacle of nature is fundamental.
If the obstacle of nature is removed, the dharmas of the first dhyāna arise.
The arising of the five factors through the eight contacts with the body is the characteristic of the first dhyāna. Within this,
that which is called "savoring" (āsvāda) is termed craving (rāga).
To be disdainful toward those who have not attained [the goal] is called pride (*māna*).
To be ignorant of suffering and its origin within dhyāna is called delusion (*moha*).
These three afflictions further comprise nine grades.
Each category consists of the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
The eight types of form-phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and the tangible objects (*spraṣṭavya*) of the desire realm, as well as the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) and so forth,
are established through causes (*hetu-siddha*).
To discern through contemplation with uninterrupted mindfulness from moment to moment is what constitutes continuity;
this arousal of the meditative mind differs from its non-arousal.
This is precisely what is meant by mutual dependence.
If one does not contemplate the destruction [of the meditative state], one will be reborn according to that dhyāna;
how then can it be called "non-arising"?
Now, by means of the skillful cultivation of the fourfold śamatha-vipaśyanā,
one advances through skillful means to sever a category of afflictions;
this is called the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga).
To realize the state free from delusion is the path of liberation.
When a portion of delusions is eliminated, cause and effect are equalized in non-arising;
this is called "entering emptiness from the conventional."
The application of the four contemplations to the continuity of dependent origination for entering emptiness through the provisional is likewise so.
Just as it is for the first chapter, it is the same for the remaining eight chapters.
Just as greed is thus destroyed, so too are pride and delusion destroyed in their nine grades.
If one destroys the obstacles of the phenomenal realm in the first dhyāna and gives rise to the intermediate state,
yet at the end of life there is no rebirth in the second dhyāna.
For example, when the nature-obstructions (*prakṛti-āvaraṇa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are not present,
the first dhyāna does not arise. Now, once the nature-obstructions of the first dhyāna are overcome, the second dhyāna immediately manifests, arising together with joy (*prīti*),
along with the four factors (*aṅga*) of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*).
Within this, there is craving for flavor, craving for existence, pride, and ignorance;
each has nine grades,
and within each grade there are three types of false designations.
When the inner pure mental object (dharmadhātu) conjoins with the mental faculty (manas),
this causal condition brings about the continuous arising of the inner pure mind.
To wait for internal purity when there is no internal purity—
this constitutes the three provisional designations.
If one does not observe or examine, but instead follows the meditative absorption to take birth.
Now, by employing śamatha and vipaśyanā in cultivation, one achieves skillful means and superior progress;
through unimpeded severance of delusions and liberation,
one realizes the truth and enters the non-arising of phenomena and principle.
If one has not yet entered [the state],
one should further contemplate the continuity and mutual dependence [of phenomena] in the same way.
The same applies to the other eight chapters.
The same also applies to delusion, pride, and so forth.
In the second dhyāna as well, there are both obstacles to objective phenomena and obstacles to the nature [of the mind].
When the activity ceases, the intermediate nature arises;
when the third dhyāna arises, it arises together with pleasure.
This pleasure is profound and subtle.
It is difficult for a noble one (*ārya*) to relinquish what an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) relinquishes.
Within this, there are nine grades of craving, pride, and delusion;
each grade contains three provisional [categories].
Pleasure corresponds to the faculty of mind (*manas*), being a continuity of a joyful mental state;
it depends upon the absence of pleasure for the presence of pleasure.
If one does not investigate, one is reborn according to the meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) one has experienced.
Now, one uses the wisdom of the fourfold contemplation to dismantle them.
Through skillful means and superior progress, one unimpededly severs delusions;
by attaining liberation and realizing the truth, one perfects the non-arising of both phenomena and principle.
If it has not yet departed,
one further cultivates the continuity and mutual dependence;
the same applies to the other eight categories as well.
The nine grades of delusion and pride are likewise.
In the third dhyāna, there are also two obstacles: those pertaining to the objective entity (*vastu*) and those pertaining to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
When the obstacle to the intrinsic nature is destroyed and equanimity (*upekṣā*) arises together with it, attachment (*rāga*), pride (*māna*), and delusion (*moha*) are also fully present.
There are also nine grades of the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*).
The immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*) corresponds to the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*),
which is established based on its causes and so forth.
If one does not observe the arising of rebirth in accordance with meditative absorption (*dhyāna*),
then by employing the skillful means of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, one advances toward the unimpeded liberation and accomplishes the principle of the non-arising of phenomena.
If [the mind] has not yet departed, one should further observe the continuity and mutual dependence in the same manner.
The same applies to the other eight categories, as well as to ignorance, pride, and so forth.
As for the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*), it is called "non-conception" because they retain form while their minds have ceased;
yet, in reality, they possess the full presence of conception.
For example, although the nature of the obstacle of karmic hindrances has been severed, the obstacle of the cognitive hindrances still remains;
one ultimately does not transcend form.
This is called a celestial being of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
Since the mind that previously broke through views has long since departed,
this mind will not arise in this heaven; rather,
it is due to the causal conditions of the matter that the mind gives rise to this meditative absorption.
There are thus the three types of conventional designations (*prajñapti*) and so forth;
these too are refuted by means of the four contemplations (*catur-vipaśyanā*).
The same applies to continuity (*saṃtati*) and mutual dependence (*apekṣā*).
If a *pañcāgāmin* deva further refines the fourth dhyāna,
using the untainted (*anāsrava*) to interpenetrate and perfume the tainted (*sāsrava*),
his form-concentration becomes increasingly luminous and his karmic fruition becomes increasingly superior.
When the supreme concentration arises,
there are also the nine grades of the three provisional afflictions— craving, pride, and delusion;
by employing the four contemplations as its essence, one realizes unimpeded liberation.
When the principle of the accomplishment of the matter is non-arising,
if it has not yet departed,
the further cultivation of the continuity of mutual dependence is likewise so.
The remaining eight categories are likewise.
Delusion and pride are also like this.
Thus, the thirty-six categories of the four [categories] of the form realm have been completed as non-arising.
Next, regarding the destruction of the nine grades of the formless realm:
when one seeks to extinguish the three kinds of form, such as the obstructive and so forth,
at that time the obstruction of objects is destroyed and the "not-yet-reached" (anāgamya) state arises.
Having destroyed the obstacle of the nature [of the form realm], one enters the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
This meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space likewise possesses craving, pride, and delusion;
yet, by employing the four contemplations as skillful means for further progress, one accomplishes the principle of the non-arising of phenomena.
If it does not depart,
the further cultivation of the continuity and mutual dependence is likewise so;
the eight categories, as well as delusion, pride, and so forth, are likewise so.
If one first takes emptiness as an object and dwells upon it excessively, the mind becomes distracted.
By relinquishing the object of emptiness and taking consciousness as the object, one attains concentration on consciousness (vijñāna-samādhi), which is associated with the mind;
this state likewise possesses afflictions such as craving, pride, and ignorance.
Furthermore, by employing the four contemplations as skillful means, one advances to accomplish the principle of the non-arising of phenomena;
other cases may be understood by analogy.
First, when the mind is concentrated on many objects of consciousness, it becomes distracted.
One abandons the consciousness that takes many objects as its condition for the sake of the consciousness of nothingness.
If it were to take few objects as its condition,
how could it be called "nothingness"?
This is because one employs a limited degree of cognition;
how, then, could it be called the "base of nothingness"?
Now, one enters meditative concentration by taking non-existence as the object-condition.
This dharma is associated with the mind;
it also possesses the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*) and so forth, and employs the four contemplations (*vipaśyanā*).
Other instances may be understood by analogy.
First, the sphere of infinite consciousness is like an abscess;
the sphere of nothingness is like a wound;
there is yet another superior meditative concentration called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The Abhidharmavibhāṣā states:
"It is not the non-perception of the Heaven of Non-Perception,
nor is it the perception of the three [formless] emptinesses."
Therefore, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The Master of Men said:
"Non-perception belongs to a different realm within the Form Realm (rūpadhātu); it should not be named after this [heaven]."
Regarding the explanation of the name within the same realm:
previously, in the concentration of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), perception (*saṃjñā*) was already eliminated;
now, furthermore, both the perception of nothingness and the perception of non-perception (*asaṃjñā*) are abandoned.
Therefore, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The first is always impure (*sāsrava*)."
The three should be distinguished:
the first three are both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*);
when they are able to give rise to supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*), they are called "without outflows."
This concentration does not give rise to the outflow-free (anāsrava);
it is exclusively with-outflows (sāsrava).
The teaching, in accordance with the capacities of those to be trained, speaks thus, sometimes concealing and sometimes revealing [the nature of this concentration].
There are those who, within this meditative absorption, give rise to the untainted (anāsrava).
How is this so? For now, let us proceed according to the teachings, and so forth.
Although this concentration is free from coarse afflictions and accomplishes ten kinds of subtle dharmas—
as described in the *Dhyanamukha*—
one should know that this concentration likewise possesses the three types of provisional existence (*prajñapti*).
Now, one employs exclusively untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) to shatter the stages of skillful means,
superior progress, unimpeded liberation, and the principle of the non-arising of accomplished matters.
The nine grades are likewise so.
The preceding examples may be understood accordingly.
If one uses worldly wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*) to sever the afflictions of volition (*saṃskāra-kleśa*), it is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*);
if one uses untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) to sever them, it is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
This is called the contemplation of the essence of thought.
To exhaust the eighty-one grades of afflictions of thought within the three realms by breaking them down is called the "pervasive destruction of dharmas."
Regarding the three knowledges (*vidyā*) that break through conceptualization to enter the stage of emptiness, there are four [sections]:

first, the stage of breaking through conceptualization according to the Tripiṭaka school; second, the stage of breaking through conceptualization according to the Shared school (*pāṭaliputra*); [third, the stage of breaking through conceptualization according to the Mahāyāna]; and fourth, the stage of breaking through conceptualization according to the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*.
Third, the distinct name for the common stage of the Universal Householder;
fourth, the distinct name for the bodhisattva stage of the Universal Householder.
Regarding the "stage of destroying conceptual thought" according to the Tripiṭaka:
The *Abhidharmakośa* clarifies that the sixteen moments of mind precisely constitute the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*).
Other schools clarify that these sixteen moments of mind belong to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
For now, we shall follow the position of the stage of cultivation.
From the abandonment of the first grade of desire-afflictions up to the exhaustion of the fifth grade,
all are termed "candidates for the fruit of once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka).
If one abandons them by leaping over [the intervening grades] up to the fifth grade, they are termed "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula).
Next, when the six grades [of afflictions] are completely severed, it is called the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
When one transcends [the lower stages] and severs up to the sixth grade, it is called "one who returns once.
Next, from the severing of the seventh grade up to the eighth grade, it is called the stage of the candidate for *anāgāmin* (*anāgāmipratipannaka*).
Transcending [the first seven grades] and reaching the eighth grade is called "one-seeded" (ekabījika).
Next, by exhausting the ninth grade, one attains the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala);
one will never again return to the desire realm.
Next, from the first category of the first dhyāna up to the eighth category of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
all seventy-one categories are termed "candidates for arhatship" (arhattva-pratipannaka).
The six types of anāgāmin stages are included therein.
In the ninth path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), the ninth affliction of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is abandoned.
In the ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one realizes the fruit of arhatship.
Having exhausted all volitional formations (*cetanā*) of the three realms, one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
The non-arising of afflictions is called "phenomenal non-arising.
Realizing the eighty-first part of true emptiness is called "principle non-arising."
The fulfillment of true wisdom is called the non-arising of wisdom;
not undergoing birth and death is called the non-arising of retribution.
If one discusses the Pratyekabuddhas:
The only difference is that the remaining minor habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) do not arise;
this is a brief summary of the determination of the stages based on the analysis of the conventional and the abandonment of volitional thought (*cetanā*).
Regarding the second point, the common stages of the three vehicles within the essence of the two penetrations (*dvividha-prativedha*):

as clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, from the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) through the stage of nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) up to the sixth stage, one shares them with the śrāvakas;
reaching the seventh stage, one shares them with the pratyekabuddhas.
Upon reaching the eighth and ninth stages, one shares in common with bodhisattvas;
when the bodhisattva stages transition into the tenth,
it is called the Buddha stage.
Regarding the statement that although they share the same stage (*sabhūmi*), there are distinctions of superior and inferior,
the treatise says:
"The three types of persons equally sever the active afflictions (*kleśa*)."
Because they enter equally into both *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder) nirvāṇa,
it is said that they are "together.
Just as there are differences such as charcoal and ash remaining after wood is burned, there are likewise distinctions of superior and inferior.
The stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) corresponds precisely to the three stages of the worthy ones (*tri-śaikṣa*).
First, the five stages of settling the mind (*pañca-sthiti-citta*);
second, the distinct-characteristic applications of mindfulness (*pṛthak-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*).
The three universal mindfulness foundations (smṛtyupasthāna) pertain generally to those outside the ranks of the noble ones (bāhyapṛthagjana); therefore,
they are called the stage of dry wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi).
"Nature" refers to the stage of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*).
By the power of the general applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one brings forth the wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) five aggregates;
this is called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
By advancing through the initial, middle, and final stages of the mind, one enters the levels of *mūrdhan*, *kṣānti*, and *laukikāgradharma*;
these are collectively termed "inner ordinary beings" (*adhyātma-prthagjana*), and are therefore called the "ground of nature" (*dharmatā-bhūmi*).
These two together subdue the afflictions of the view-obscurations.
"The eight persons" refers to the eight patiences (*kṣānti*).
From the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), one transitions into the "uninterrupted samādhi" (*ānantarya-samādhi*).
Therefore, they are called the "Eight Persons.
As for the "Stage of Seeing," because those who see perceive the Truth and sever all eighty-eight afflictions (*āśrava*) of the three realms of existence,
it is called the Stage of Seeing.
The "Thin" (Tanu) stage is so named because one eliminates six grades of afflictions through contemplation within the desire realm;
the "Detached from Desire" (Vītarāga) stage is so named because one eliminates all nine grades within the desire realm.
Therefore, it is called the stage of detachment from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*).
As for "having completed" (*kṛtāvin*), this refers to the elimination of the seventy-two categories of afflictions pertaining to the form and formless realms;
because it is like fire burning wood into charcoal, it is called the stage of having completed what was to be done (*kṛtāvi-bhūmi*).
As for the Pratyekabuddha,
his merit and wisdom are so profound and sharp that he is able to eradicate habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) as if burning wood to ashes.
As for the Bodhisattva...
The paths of merit and wisdom, profound and sharp, flow together as a dual stream;
one severs habitual tendencies and the ignorance of both form and mind,
thereby attaining the Dharma-eye and the knowledge of the modes of the path.
They sport with supernatural powers and purify Buddha-fields;
they study the dharmas such as the powers and fearlessnesses of a Buddha;
their residual habits are nearly exhausted, like a small amount of remaining ash.
The Buddha-ground is that which,
through the accumulation of great merit and wisdom, attains the wisdom of a single moment of correspondence;
its habitual tendencies are forever exhausted, like the fire at the end of an eon when there is neither charcoal nor ash remaining.
This refers to the stage where the afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) are severed through the ten stages common to the three vehicles.
Regarding the distinct names for these stages that are shared by the general tradition,
the older texts state:
Some say that views are abandoned at the third stage;
others say they are abandoned at the fourth stage;
and others say that the cessation of all thought occurs at the sixth stage.
Some say that the afflictions of thought are exhausted at the seventh stage.
Now, let us examine these words.
If it is claimed that both the third and fourth stages eliminate all views, [then...]
This master does not understand the meaning of the Shared Teaching (sādhāraṇa-śāsana). Why?
Because [practitioners of] the three vehicles occupy the same stage and together enter the samādhi of immediate succession (ānantarya-samādhi).
If one does not enter or emerge from contemplation to sever views,
why suddenly employ the third and fourth stages to sever them?
If one were to take only the third stage as that which severs views, [what would become of the others?]
In the fourth stage, one should abandon conceptualization (*vitarka*).
If it were the case that only the views (*dṛṣṭi*) are abandoned in the fourth stage,
then the views would not yet have been abandoned in the third stage.
If one uses the two stages to sever views as the point of entering and emerging from meditative absorption,
then if it is not a case of entering and emerging from absorption, those two stages do not exist;
if it is a case of entering and emerging from absorption, it is not the stage of severing views.
The Master Ren-shi attempted to rescue [his position] by saying,
"The sutra speaks thus.
This master did not understand the intent of the sutra.
Now it is said:
the sutra borrows specific meanings to reveal the general;
the specific meaning of "vision" (darśana) is elaborated upon in the treatise regarding the third and fourth stages.
While the meaning of "penetration" (tong) refers to the deficiency of not entering or emerging from meditative absorption,
the name may be borrowed for a specific sense, yet its essential meaning must rely on the general one.
If one were to provide an interpretation of it as not entering or emerging from absorption, [it would contradict the definition].
If one says "the third stage," it is based on the initial moment of severing views;
if one says "the fourth stage," it is based on the period following the severance of views.
In neither case does one emerge from meditative observation.
For example, regarding the sixteenth moment of mind, some call it the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
while others call it the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
To say that a specific name is used to designate a general stage means:
The three levels of the outer ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana) are the stage of dry wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi),
which are termed the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā).
The four roots of goodness (catvāri kuśalamūlāni) of the inner ordinary beings (adhyātma-pṛthagjana) constitute the stage of nature (gotra-bhūmi).
These are termed the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications.
The stage of the eight persons and the stage of insight are the stage of Srotāpanna,
which is termed the first stage, the Stage of Joy.
The Stage of Thinness (tanubhūmi) corresponds to the Sakṛdāgāmin;
the Sakṛdāgāmin comprises both the candidate for the fruit and the possessor of the fruit.
Establishing the candidate as the Stainless Stage (vimalābhūmi).
Establishing the fruit as the Ground of Illumination (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
The Ground of Freedom from Desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*) is the stage of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
The Non-returner possesses both the path of approach (*pratipannaka*) and the fruit (*phala*).
Establishing the orientation is the Ground of Radiance (Arciṣmatī).
Establishing the fruit is the Ground Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā).
The Ground of Having Accomplished (Kṛtāvī) is the stage of the Arhat.
The Arhat has both the path of approach (mārga) and the fruit (phala).
The path of approach is established as the Bhūmi of Presence (Abhimukhī),
and the fruit is established as the Bhūmi of Far-Going (Dūraṅgamā).
The stage of the Pratyekabuddha is established as the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi),
and the Bodhisattva grounds are established as the Ground of Excellent Wisdom (Sādhumatī-bhūmi).
Alternatively, the final mind of the Bodhisattva grounds is established as the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).
Alternatively, the Buddha-ground may be taken as the Dharma-cloud ground (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"A Bodhisattva of the tenth ground is like a Buddha."
This interpretation can thus be established.
If one were to use these specific names to judge the general stages of the three types of persons,
then it would follow that the first stage (bhūmi) eliminates the delusions of views.
In the second stage, one abandons one or two categories of volitions of the desire realm;
in the third stage, one abandons six categories of volitions;
in the fourth stage, one abandons seven or eight categories of volitions.
On the fifth stage, one abandons nine grades of thought;
on the sixth stage, seventy-one grades of thought;
and on the seventh stage, seventy-two grades of thought.
From the eighth stage upward, the afflictions, habitual tendencies, ignorance, and so forth are severed;
this may be understood by analogy with what was stated previously, and so on.
Fourth, regarding the use of specific names to designate the general stages of a bodhisattva:
Dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) belongs to the external stage of the ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
The stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*) belongs to the internal stage of the ordinary person.
The eight persons constitute the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*).
The fifteen moments of mind constitute the second stage;
the sixteenth moment of mind constitutes the third stage.
In these three stages, one eliminates the delusions of view without emerging from meditative contemplation.
The four patiences constitute the first stage;
the four knowledges constitute the second stage;
and the four subsequent patiences constitute the third stage.
The four subsequent knowledges (*anvaya-jñāna*) constitute the four stages (*bhūmi*).
In these four stages, one eliminates the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) without emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
If explained in this manner, how could it not differ from the traditional [explanation], and so forth?
The "Thin" [stage] consists of abandoning six grades of thought in the fifth dhyāna;
the "Detachment from Desire" consists of abandoning nine grades of thought in the sixth dhyāna;
and the "Accomplished" consists of exhausting all thoughts of the form and formless realms in the seventh dhyāna.
The Pratyekabuddha corresponds to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
Up to the Buddha-stage, one eliminates the residual habits and non-cognitive ignorance;
this follows the same pattern as previously explained, and so forth.
The old [commentary] states:
"In the sixth stage, the severing of thought is exhausted, equaling that of an Arhat.
Alternatively, according to the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-vidyā-rāja-sūtra*, it is stated that "in the seventh stage, one equals an Arhat."
However, the sixth stage is termed "detachment from desire.
This merely involves detachment from the nine grades of the desire realm and can at best be equated with the stage of an Anāgāmin.
Even if one proceeds while still carrying the fruit,
as long as there remains the ninth grade of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception,
one cannot yet be equated with an Arhat.
If it were the case that the seventh stage constitutes "having already accomplished" (kṛtābhisamaya) with respect to the fruit,
then since the first category of the first dhyāna would already belong to the seventh stage,
one would have attained the name "already accomplished" at that time.
Now, if we adopt the interpretation that facilitates understanding,
the meaning is clarified by way of the ten perfections;
therein, the sixth perfection, prajñā, is the wisdom that enters into emptiness.
Having severed all delusions, one is equal to an Arhat.
The seventh stage involves the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*) emerging from the conventional to manifest transformative activity;
this is designated as "skillful means" (*upāya*).
If one takes the seventh stage as being equal to the Arhat,
then in terms of correlating the various stages with the fruits and the paths toward those fruits,
the seventh stage is precisely equal to the fourth fruit.
These are all provisional correspondences;
since the sūtras and śāstras are not definitive,
one must further exercise careful discernment.
"One must not dogmatically cling [to this view]," and so forth.
Question:
The meaning of the common abandonment by the three vehicles has already been clarified.
On what basis do you further claim that the Bodhisattva-bhūmi alone is opened?
Answer:
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* judges that there are three stages for the wick to burn out;
thus, there are three types of bodhisattvas who sever delusions.
The stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) is the subduing of delusions.
It is still possible for this to be considered the first *āpatti* (offense).
Now, if one takes the true severance [of defilements] by these eight persons as the first *āpatti*, what is the harm? And so forth.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* clarifies that a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage is like a Buddha.
Since it clarifies that the final stage is adjacent to the ultimate,
how could there not be the intermediate stages and the first stage?
Inferring from this,
what fault is there in separately establishing the ten stages (bhūmi) of a bodhisattva?
If these ten stages did not exist, [what would be the consequence?]
The Sūtra should not state that a bodhisattva cultivates the karmas of the stages from the first stage to the tenth stage,
with each stage having such-and-such dharma-gates, and so forth.
Furthermore, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra says:
The stage of dry wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi) is the patience of subduing (avaivartika-kṣānti) regarding the dharmas of a bodhisattva;
the stage of nature (gotra-bhūmi) is the patience of compliance (anuloma-kṣānti) regarding the dharmas of a bodhisattva;
and the stage of the eight persons (aṣṭamaka-bhūmi) is the patience of non-arising (anutpāda-kṣānti) regarding a bodhisattva.
For a bodhisattva, the stage of seeing is the fruit of the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
For a bodhisattva, the stage of thinning is called the purity of freedom from desire (*vairāgya-viśuddhi*).
For a bodhisattva, the stage of freedom from desire is called the playful mastery of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-krīḍana*).
The stage of "having already accomplished" (*kṛtāvibhūmi*) is called the Buddha-stage for Śrāvakas,
whereas for Bodhisattvas it is the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*). Therefore,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
Whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to a stream-enterer—
that is the bodhisattva’s acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
This extends even to whatever wisdom or abandonment belongs to a pratyekabuddha.
This is the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). As in this treatise,
it has already been distinguished specifically with respect to the bodhisattva.
Now, what fault is there in establishing this interpretation?
Question:
The desire realm also involves the abandonment of the nine grades.
With what intention is it judged that the fruit is manifold?
Answer:
Just as a dangerous place has many difficulties and thus requires many walls.
It is because of the many obstacles and many fruits within the realms that there is cessation from them.
If that is so, why are the dhyānas established as being free from distraction and possessing many requirements?
Answer:
In the desire realm and in non-concentrated stages, dhyāna cannot be established;
however, the fruit can be established through the universal attainment of the outflow-free (anāsrava) object.
Question:

Question: Since the wisdom and abandonment of those of the three vehicles are equal, why are those of the two vehicles called "wisdom and abandonment" (jñāna-prahāṇa), while Bodhisattvas are called "dharma-patience" (dharma-kṣānti)?
Answer:
Patience is the cause and wisdom is the fruit;
therefore, fifteen moments of mind are called patience,
and the sixteenth moment of mind is called wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding the realization of the two vehicles, it is appropriate to judge them by their wisdom and abandonment;
as for the bodhisattva, since they still abide in the causal stage relative to the Buddha,
they receive only the name of "patience" (kṣānti).
Furthermore, when a single stage of a bodhisattva’s contemplation is exhausted,
a corresponding portion of mastery arises;
thus, they die stage by stage and are reborn stage by stage.
It is called "patience" (kṣānti) because one is able to endure the toil and suffering of birth and death without entering nirvāṇa.
If one explains the stage of breaking through conceptualization and the provisional according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao),
one first breaks through views and correctly enters the First Abode (prathamavihāra).
From the second stage through the seventh stage, one breaks through the conceptualization of the provisional;
if one wishes to further subdivide the categories to distinguish the various stages,
it may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
From the eighth, ninth, and tenth abodes (*vihāra*) onward is precisely the stage of "infiltrating and practicing" (*qinxí*).
The ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) are precisely the stage of "correctly exiting into the provisional" (*chūjiǎ*).
They no longer concern what preceded them, and so forth.
If one approaches the stage of breaking through the provisional based on the Perfect Teaching,
the initial breaking through the provisional of views corresponds precisely to the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*).
From the second stage of faith up to the seventh stage of faith constitutes the breaking through the provisional of thought (*vitarka*).
If one wishes to subdivide the ranks to correspond with the various stages of faith,
it may be understood by analogy with what preceded.
From the eighth faith to the tenth faith, the residual habits (*vāsanā*) are completely eradicated.
The *Avataṃsaka* states:
"At the moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], the fundamental afflictions (*āsrava*) and their habitual tendencies (*vāsana*) are simultaneously exhausted without remainder.
However, outside of this realm, the fundamental afflictions and their habitual tendencies are not yet fully exhausted.
This refers simply to the complete exhaustion of both the fundamental afflictions and their habitual tendencies within the realm of phenomena (*dhātu*).
As the *Avataṃsaka* states:
"From the very first aspiration, one has already surpassed the Muni."
This is precisely that meaning.
What is the fault? It would mean that both the active defilements (*vāsana*) and those already cultivated are simultaneously exhausted.
One is able to manifest Buddhahood through the eight aspects;
in this regard, they are equal.
Furthermore, the three contemplations are cultivated in their entirety.
This would mean that [the Bodhisattva] has surpassed them. If that were so,
then there should also be Śrāvakas who surpass Bodhisattvas.
Nevertheless, the path of the Buddha and that of the śrāvaka are clearly superior to that of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, while the preceding stages are identical in their deconstruction of provisional designations,
they differ in their application of wisdom in taking principle as the object-condition.
The Tripitaka and the Shared Teachings, among others, involve the Two Vehicles' refutation of the provisional;
at the time of death according to worldly truth,
they cannot emerge from the provisional and lack mastery over rebirth.
When a Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) has shattered the provisional and passes away according to the conventional truth (shidi),
they are still able to emerge from the provisional state and take birth with mastery.
When the conditions for transformation are exhausted,
one dissolves the body to realize emptiness;
this is the provisional teaching that destroys the false.
At the time of death according to conventional truth,
one is also able to emerge from the provisional and take birth with mastery,
thereby manifesting that the Middle Way ultimately does not abide in emptiness.
In the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*),
when shattering the provisional, seeing the true is simultaneously entering the provisional and entering the middle.
Thus, one perfectly subdues ignorance (*avidyā*).
If one says that the wisdom and abandonment of the two vehicles and those of the bodhisattvas are identical, while they differ in terms of transforming others,
this is merely a comparison based on the intent of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao).
If one says that the wisdom of the two vehicles and that of the bodhisattvas differ, while their abandonment is the same, [this is also a specific distinction].
This is merely a comparison between the Separate and the Perfect [vehicles].
Question:
One breaks through the provisional to enter emptiness by destroying conceptual thought.
In total, there are eighty-one grades to be broken.
Why, then, is there the principle of "transcending the fruit"?
Answer:
Although there is a sequential enumeration of the preceding items,
the practitioner does not necessarily enter them strictly according to their order.
This is as in the case of the sixteen moments of mind following [the path of seeing] within the Tripiṭaka.
Then, in a single thought-moment, one may leap beyond the fruit to reach the stage of Anāgāmin,
or leap further to reach Arhatship;
how could there be any further gradual progression as previously enumerated?
Although one does not sequentially pass through all the stages, the afflictions of all stages are exhausted,
and the meditative concentrations of all stages arise, and so forth.
It is also like the Buddha of the Tripiṭaka.
In a single thought-moment of correspondence, the afflictions of views and thoughts are suddenly exhausted,
and the merits of the Buddha manifest all at once;
because the faculties are sharp, this occurs without passing through the successive stages.
Although one's benefit may transcend various ranks, one must not neglect them. Why is this?
Because such is the nature of the Dharma-gates of all Buddhas.
Question:
Those with sharp faculties are able to transcend [the stages].
Śāriputra possessed the sharpest faculties; for what reason did he not transcend them?
Answer:
The Lesser Vehicle leads those of dull faculties to rest;
therefore, they do not transcend.
Śāriputra, possessing great wisdom, was to serve as the general who turns the wheel of Dharma;
therefore, he did not exceed seven days— or, according to some accounts, fifteen days— in distinguishing their respective ranks.
Because Ānanda served as his attendant,
he did not transcend [the realm of desire];
it was not that he lacked the power of wisdom.
The bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) possess wisdom that surpasses that of the two vehicles;
they should likewise have transcendence,
for they shoulder the burden of sentient beings and act as their leaders.
Because it requires extensive differentiation, the "leap-over" (chao) is not discussed;
the same applies to the two teachings of Separate (bie) and Perfect (yuan).
Although there are instances of leaping over and not leaping over, [the distinction remains].
In the end, this is the breaking of conceptual thought and the universalization of the provisional.
There are four types of transcendence regarding the fruit:
first, transcendence through fundamental severance.
Second, the minor leap-over;
third, the great leap-over;
fourth, the great-great leap-over.
Originally abiding in the stage of an ordinary person, one attains the meditative attainment of non-perception;
now, with the fulfillment of the sixteenth moment of untainted mind,
one immediately attains the state of a Non-returner (Anāgāmin).
Originally abiding in the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), one may have attained the first dhyāna, or the second, third, or fourth dhyānas;
now, with the completion of the sixteen moments of mind, one is likewise an Anāgāmin.

Originally abiding in the stage of an ordinary person in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), one eliminates the nine grades [of afflictions] through mundane wisdom (laukikajñāna) to whatever extent; at the completion of the sixteenth moment of mind, one becomes an Anāgāmin.
Attaining the fruit by transcending through the abandonment of the fundamental stage is all termed "transcending the fundamental abandonment.
This applies when an ordinary person has not yet attained dhyāna on the mundane level.
When the sixteen moments of mind are fulfilled,
one is able to transcend and simultaneously eliminate various categories of the desire realm,
whether three or two categories.
This refers to those such as the "house-to-house" (kulaṃkula) and the "one-seed" (ekabījika), which constitute the "small leap.
Originally abiding in the stage of ordinary beings, they heard the Dharma and were addressed with the call, "Welcome! (svāgata).
One who has become an Arhat is one who has "greatly transcended"; just as for a Buddha,
in a single thought-moment, both active afflictions and residual habits are completely exhausted.
This is called the Greatly Transcendent.
The person of the Perfect Teaching possesses the sharpest faculties.
Furthermore, this is the ultimate teaching and is without hierarchical gradations.
This is most capable of transcending [all stages].
The *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* clarifies that the Tathāgata is attained through sudden enlightenment;
the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that one attains perfect awakening in a single kṣaṇa.
According to this principle, there is transcendence;
however, because the compassionate vows are so profound and weighty, one does not transcend them.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* says:
Although one attains the Buddha-way and delivers sentient beings while practicing the bodhisattva path,
this is both transcending and not transcending.
In the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), there is neither transcending nor non-transcending.
"If one follows chance, there is universal movement; if one accords with principle, there is constant stillness," and so forth.
Regarding the "Analysis of the Four and Three Gates":
Now, the two delusions of views and thought obstruct the two principles of the general and the specific.
If one breaks through obstacles to reveal the principle, there is no gate that is not penetrated.
As clarified in the Abhidharma:
the self, the person, and sentient beings are as unfindable as the hair of a tortoise or the horns of a rabbit; there exist only real dharmas.
Deluded regarding this true dharma, they give rise in vain to views and afflictions.
These views and afflictions are impermanent, not abiding for even a single moment;
the true dharma is shifting and moving, undergoing birth and extinction in every fraction of an instant.
One who contemplates in this manner is able to destroy all views— whether single, dual, or complete—
and likewise destroys the eighty-one grades of afflictions within the three realms.
Thus, the causal and resultant delusions and wisdoms become non-arising.
This is called the intent of the "Gate of Existence" within the Tripiṭaka for refuting [wrong] dharmas.
When the Deer Park was first opened,
the five men led by Kauṇḍinya were the first to attain purity.
Furthermore, when Ājñātakauṇḍinya expounded the Three Truths,
Śāriputra shattered his views;
seven days later, he attained arhatship.
More than twelve hundred [monks] perceived the ultimate truth through the gate of existence.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If one attains the skillful means of prajñā..."
Entering the Abhidharma, one does not fall into existence.
The Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says:
"Those who hold to the view of permanence claim that distinct thoughts are severed."
This is precisely the meaning of severing the fetters at the stage of the "stream-enterer" (srotāpanna).
Is this not the intention of the "Gate of Existence" (yǒumén) to dismantle conventional designations?
Why do the followers of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* dismiss it, saying that it is merely a skillful means for disciplining the mind and does not lead to the Path?
According to what is elucidated in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the self and the person fundamentally do not exist; although real dharmas exist, they are fleeting and non-existent.
If one is deluded regarding these fleeting [dharmas], [one clings to them as substantial].
Transversely arising views and afflictions cause one to transmigrate through birth and death;
yet when observing these views and afflictions, they are all seen to be floating and hollow, consisting of the three kinds of provisional existence,
wherein both the provisional and the real are non-existent.
This is called the emptiness of equality.
By cultivating such contemplation, one destroys the infinite views— both single, dual, and combined—
as well as the eighty-one grades of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
The non-arising of afflictions, wisdom, cause, effect,
and so forth is called the meaning of the "Dharma-destroying" intent of the Emptiness Gate within the Tripiṭaka.
Therefore, that treatise states:
I now intend to clarify the true meaning within the Tripitaka.
That which is the true meaning is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
As the Āgama Sūtra says:
To ask "Who is it that ages and dies? or "What is it that ages and dies?
are both wrong views.
This aging and death is itself the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).
"Whoever undergoes old age and death is empty of a sentient being.
Furthermore, it says:
"The Buddha’s Dharma-body is itself emptiness."
Subhūti’s wisdom regarding emptiness was particularly clear;
he was thus able to perceive the Buddha’s Dharma-body within a stone chamber.
For this reason, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* specifically emphasizes the teaching of emptiness.
Śāriputra was addressed with an exposition of Prajñāpāramitā because the Buddha wished to pair the Great Emptiness with the Small Emptiness,
and Great Wisdom with Small Wisdom.
Therefore, these two persons were commissioned to teach in turn.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If one does not obtain the skillful means of *prajñā*, one cannot enter emptiness."
They fall into the midst of non-existence.
The *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* states:
"Those who hold the view of annihilationism claim that [existence] is severed in a single thought-moment."
Is this not the meaning of the equality of emptiness?

One should know that the people of the Abhidharma school of the Tripiṭaka further explain the gate of emptiness, saying: "How can one sweep away [all phenomena]—this is the meaning of the Great Vehicle’s emptiness.
This is as Kātyāyanīputra set forth the gateway through which he entered.
The *Kun-le lun zhuan* (Treatise on the *Kośa*) states that in South India,
the provisional [teachings] are as before,
while the real dharmas are both existent and non-existent.
If, upon arising from meditative concentration, views and afflictions arise crosswise,
one observes this real dharma with composure regarding its existence or non-existence; thus,
one also breaks the eighty-one types of views and afflictions, including those that are single or combined.

The non-arising of the causes and effects of afflictions and wisdom is called the "Gate of Both Emptiness and Existence" within the Tripiṭaka; this is the intent behind the deconstruction of phenomena.
Thus, the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra states:
If one attains the skillful means of Prajñā to enter the gate of the *kun-lê* (Dharmadhātu),
one does not fall into the extremes of existence or non-existence;
this is the gate that is neither empty nor existent.
As clarified in the *Śāstra*, since Candaka’s mind has become disciplined and supple,
you should preach to him the *Nandakagāndhārī-sūtra*:
that one attains the Way by departing from both existence and non-existence.
This contemplation is also able to shatter the eighty-one modes of thought associated with both simple and compound views.
By entering from the conventional into emptiness, one realizes that the causes and effects of afflictions and wisdom are equally non-arising;
this is precisely the intent of the Three Piṭaka’s gate of "neither existence nor non-existence" in refuting the conventional.
One should know that Chanda attained the path of the Hīnayāna;
he must not be conflated with the gateway of the Middle Way of the Mahāyāna.
These four gateways are all referred to as those who have attained the path of the Srotāpanna.
Because the *śrotāpanna* (stream-enterer) is the first fruit,
those who excel further receive distinct names,
resulting in the differentiation of three gates.
One also attains mastery over these channels:
the channel of impermanence with gates,
and the channel of the equality of emptiness without gates.
The gate of "both existent and non-existent" leads to the *śrotāpanna* (Stream-enterer) stage;
the gate of "neither existent nor non-existent" also leads to the *śrotāpanna* stage.
The *śrotāpanna* is the initial fruit of all four gates.
The four gates differ in their observations, yet the vision of the True Truth (satyadharma) is the same.
It is like a city with four gates that converge upon one point without distinction.
Thus, the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says:

sentient beings are likewise.

regarding all phenomena, one does not accept them and thus becomes an Arhat.
As previously explained, one completely does not accept any of the views, whether single or compound.

alternatively, five dharmas serve as medicine, namely the five powers;

the eightfold noble path,
and the nine perceptions.

Bodhisattvas who have emerged from the provisional realm must all recognize this:
for the sake of sentient beings, they gather the medicinal herbs of the various dharmas,
like a master mariner at sea.
If one does not know [this], one cannot benefit sentient beings;
therefore, in order to gain such knowledge, one should single-mindedly and comprehensively cultivate both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*,
along with the power of great compassionate vows and diligence.
The majestic power of all Buddhas causes their Dharma-eye to be opened and developed,
enabling them to understand all things as clearly as if observing fruit in the palm of their hand;
furthermore, they know the world-transcending, supreme medicinal herbs of the Dharma.
Regarding the single dharma of śamatha-vipaśyanā as medicine:
this refers to the one true reality (ekasatyatā).
When the mind of ignorance merges with the dharmatā, all manner of pathological signs arise.
When one contemplates this dharma-nature, even the dharma-nature itself does not exist;
how much less so ignorance and all other dharmas?
Alternatively, these two dharmas as medicine are precisely śamatha and vipaśyanā.
One realizes that the nature of the mind is illusory and brings it to rest;
alternatively, the three dharmas serve as medicine, namely śamatha and vipaśyanā,
along with the precepts that follow the Path, which provide spontaneous protection.
Furthermore, there are three samādhis:
entering from the conventional into emptiness is called the emptiness samādhi;
not perceiving even the mark of emptiness is called the signless samādhi.
The cessation of the karma of birth and death is called the *asaṃskṛta-samādhi* (the samādhi of non-action).
Alternatively, the four dharmas serve as the medicine, namely the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*).
All views depend upon form (*rūpa*).
This form is neither defiled nor non-defiled;
the various views and thoughts are neither suffering nor pleasure;
the various views, perceptions, and formations are neither self nor non-self.
Since even the minds of various views and afflictions are not truly mind,
how could they be either permanent or impermanent?
Alternatively, the five dharmas as medicine are themselves the five faculties.
To be free from doubt while practicing śamatha and vipaśyanā is called the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya).
To constantly mindfully attend to śamatha and vipaśyanā without attending to other matters is the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya).
The uninterrupted practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā is the faculty of diligence (vīryendriya).
One-pointed concentration in samādhi is the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya).
Thoroughly penetrating the four propositions as being without intrinsic nature is the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya).
The growth of the five faculties is called the five powers.
Alternatively, six dharmas serve as medicine, namely the six foundations of mindfulness.
Through the awakening of cessation and contemplation, one perceives that the afflictions of thought and emotion are themselves the Buddha-dharma realm.
Not breaking the dharma-body is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
Constantly recollecting and maintaining śamatha and vipaśyanā, without discriminating between the characteristics of their unity or difference,
is called mindfulness of the Dharma.
The harmony of the principles of śamatha and vipaśyanā is the characteristic of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta);
therefore, it is called "recollection of the Saṅgha.
Within śamatha and vipaśyanā, there is the morality that accords with the Path (mārgānuloma-śīla).
This is called mindfulness of the precepts.
Stopping and contemplation are the ultimate truth;
this is called mindfulness of the heavens.
The cessation of the afflictions of views and thoughts through śamatha and vipaśyanā is called "mindfulness-abandonment" (*smṛti-prahāṇa*).
Alternatively, these seven factors serve as the medicine.
Calm abiding (*śamatha*) consists of the factors of concentration (*samādhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Insight (*vipaśyanā*) consists of the factors of discernment (*pravicaya*), joy (*prīti*), and vigor (*vīrya*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) pertains to both.
Alternatively, the eight factors serve as the medicine.
The fourfold analysis that deconstructs conventional designations constitutes right view;
the activation and arousal of this right view is termed contemplation (*cintā*).
Practicing in accordance with this is called right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
Explaining this calm abiding and insight is called right speech (*samyag-vāc*).
Sustaining the body without deceit or guile is called right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
Non-distraction and non-forgetfulness are called right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
Cessation is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
Uninterrupted mindfulness is called diligence (*vīrya*).
Alternatively, there are nine factors that serve as medicine:
namely, the four views regarding the impurity of the five aggregates;

Knowing the distinctions among all phenomena is the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*).
Knowing the exhaustion of suffering and its origin is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*);
untainted wisdom is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
